summary_of_pdf: This document constitutes a formal demand letter and notice of pending patent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 154(d) directed at the chief executives and chief legal officers of major automotive manufacturers. The claimant, Reinaldo J. Aguiar Marcano, asserts that the automotive industry's transition to Software-Defined Vehicles (SDVs)—specifically utilizing optical data buses, Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) optical communication, and EV cybersecurity protocols—will infringe upon his portfolio of thirty-three pending USPTO applications. The notice seeks to establish actual knowledge to trigger the accrual of provisional rights for reasonable royalties and demands immediate Freedom to Operate (FTO) audits, the quarantine of intersecting technologies, and engagement in licensing negotiations within thirty days.
attorneys_comments: From a tactical and evidentiary standpoint, this correspondence attempts to lay the foundational predicate for provisional damages under 35 U.S.C. § 154(d). However, the evidentiary strength of this notice is highly suspect and procedurally premature. Section 154(d) strictly requires actual notice of a *published* patent application. The claimant explicitly states these applications were filed in March 2026, while this notice is dated April 9, 2026. Under standard USPTO procedure (35 U.S.C. § 122(b)), applications are not published until 18 months post-filing unless expedited publication is specifically requested and granted. Thus, the claims are likely unpublished, rendering the § 154(d) notice legally defective for accruing provisional royalties at this juncture. Furthermore, the broad, sweeping nature of the infringement allegations against entire industry roadmaps lacks the requisite claim chart specificity expected in federal practice. Procedurally, this functions as a high-risk, aggressive licensing tactic. If the recipient companies perceive a genuine, immediate controversy, this letter provides ample jurisdictional basis for them to file a declaratory judgment action for non-infringement or invalidity under 28 U.S.C. § 2201, potentially dragging the claimant into a forum of the automakers' choosing. The lack of issued patents means no immediate injunctive relief or standard infringement damages under 35 U.S.C. § 271 are available.
recommended_next_steps: 1. Docket the receipt of this notice and preserve all related correspondence to maintain a pristine evidentiary record. 2. Task patent prosecution counsel to monitor the USPTO Patent Center for the publication of the cited application serial numbers (19/562,818; 19/560,038; 19/560,042; 19/574,356; 19/560,069; 19/560,062) to assess actual claim scope once public. 3. Conduct a preliminary internal Freedom to Operate (FTO) review focusing on the specific hardware (optical data buses, LED matrix V2V telemetry) to preemptively identify prior art. 4. Refrain from substantive engagement or licensing negotiations at this time, as responding may inadvertently concede the validity of the notice or ripen a declaratory judgment controversy. 5. Prepare a standard non-infringement and premature notice response template should the claimant escalate, explicitly noting the failure to meet the publication requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 154(d).
